deep.reconstruction:
This page continues the table on the neighbouring folios (the next page is headed 'Verwandlung gemeiner Brüche in Decimalbrüche'). For the primes p = 409, 419, 421, 431, 433 and 439 Gauss writes out the full repeating periods of fractions a/p, in groups of ten digits.

Convention. The period of 1/p begins '00…' when p > 100. Gauss drops the first zero, so the string he writes is the period of 10/p. For example, 10/409 = 0.0244498777…, and that period ends '…5110'. A period of length e = ord_p(10) splits the p−1 nonzero residues into k = (p−1)/e cosets of <10>. Gauss writes one period per coset.

(1) p = 409. ord(10) = 204, so k = 2.
- First period: 9+9+2 groups plus '9144', which is 204 digits. It begins 2542787286…, the expansion of 104/409.
- Second period: 204 digits, the period of 10/409 = 0.0244498777 5061124694 … 0440097799 5110.
- Since 10^102 ≡ −1 (mod 409), each period is self-complementary: digit k+102 = 9 − digit k. Example: digits 103–112 are 9755501222, the complement of 0244498777.

(2) p = 419. ord(10) = 418, so 10 is a primitive root and there is one period of 4·90 + 58 = 418 digits, starting 0238663484 (10/419). Since 10^209 ≡ −1, digit k+209 = 9 − digit k.

(3) p = 421. ord(10) = 140, so k = 3 and there are three periods of 9+5 groups = 140 digits each:
- 2826603325… = 119/421;
- 2636579572… = 111/421;
- 0237529691… = 10/421.

(4) p = 431. ord(10) = 215, which is odd, so k = 2.
- First period: 4872389791… = 210/431, 215 digits ending '31090'.
- Second period: 0232018561… = 10/431, ending '25290'.
- Because the order is odd, −1 is not in <10>, so the second coset is −<10>. The two periods are therefore 9's-complements of each other up to rotation. Check: complement(0232018561) = 9767981438, complement(4849187935) = 5150812064, complement(0348027842) = 9651972157. All three appear consecutively inside the first period: '…3874709976 7981438515 0812064965 1972157772…'.

(5) p = 433. 10 is a primitive root; one period of 360 + 72 = 432 digits, starting 0230946882 (10/433).

(6) p = 439. ord(10) = 219, odd, so k = 2.
- First period: 4920273348… = 216/439, 219 digits. Its last line ends in a struck-out group.
- Second period: 0227790432… = 10/439, ending '847380410'.
- The complement relation again holds: complement(0227790432) = 9772209567, which appears at '…5899 7722095671…'; complement(8018223234) = 1981776765, at '…671 9817767653…'.
- The pencil note 'HH 5968109339 407' (in a different hand, possibly an editor's) restores the end of line 1 of the first period, lost to the torn edge. The group is 5968109339, and the next line begins 407…
- 'C546' is presumably an archival or count mark.

The purpose is to build the table of decimal periods for prime denominators described in Disquisitiones Arithmeticae arts. 312–318. With the periods of a few numerators per prime (one per coset of <10>), any fraction a/p can be converted by finding a's coset and the offset within it.
errors: p = 419, line 5, group 2 (digits 371–380) reads '1183317422' in the image and transcription. The complement relation (digit k+209 = 9 − digit k, with digits 162–171 = 8806682577) gives 1193317422, so this is likely a copying slip (8 for 9) by Gauss or the reader.

p = 439, first period: the last group of line 3 has a stray extra digit ('503416856' with a trailing '4'?), and the following group is struck out. The period closes at 219 digits with '503416856'. This is a self-correction, not an error left standing.
No other inconsistencies were found in the spot checks: period lengths for all six primes, and the complement relations for 409, 419, 431 and 439.

results.what: Full decimal periods of 10/p and of representatives of the other cosets of <10> mod p, for p = 409, 419, 421, 431, 433, 439. Multiplicative orders 204, 418, 140, 215, 432, 219.
results.modern_name: Tables of decimal expansions / periods of 1/p; multiplicative order of 10 mod p; cosets of the subgroup <10> in (Z/pZ)*
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss, Disquisitiones Arithmeticae (1801), arts. 312–318; his table for denominators below 1000 was published in Werke II (1863). Earlier tables by J. H. Lambert and J. Bernoulli; later Burckhardt, Reuschle, Cunningham.

results.what: Complement structure: for odd ord_p(10) the two periods are 9's-complements of each other; for even order each period is self-complementary at its half-length.
results.modern_name: Midy's theorem and its coset generalisation (10^(e/2) ≡ −1 mod p)
results.usually_credited_to: E. Midy (1836); the property was known earlier, including from Gauss's treatment in DA

deep.surprise_reason: This is a worksheet for Gauss's well-known table of decimal periods, published in Werke II and described in Disquisitiones arts. 312–318. It is computational raw material with no new theory.

checkable.asserts: The period lengths implied by the number of digits Gauss writes for each prime.
Digits 201–204 of 10/409 are 5110, closing the 204-digit period as written.
The three 421 periods begin with 119/421, 111/421 and 10/421.
The two 431 periods begin with 210/431 and 10/431.
The two 439 periods begin with 216/439 and 10/439.
10^(e/2) ≡ −1, giving the self-complementary periods for 409 and 419.
Evaluates digits 101–110 of 10/439. Compare with 9840546697, the 6th group of line 2 of the first 439 period, after locating the offset (spot check of the complement rotation).
